Submission received: 31 March 2025 / Revised: 8 May 2025 / Accepted: 12 May 2025 / Published: 14 May 2025 Abstract As fossil fuel depletion and environmental pollution become increasingly severe, biodiesel has emerged as a promising renewable alternative to conventional diesel due to its biodegradability, low sulfur emissions, and high combustion efficiency. This paper provides a comprehensive review of the evolution of biodiesel feedstocks, major production technologies, and key factors influencing production efficiency and fuel quality. It traces the development of feedstocks from first-generation edible oils, second-generation non-edible oils and waste fats, to third-generation microalgal oils and fourth-generation biofuels based on synthetic biology, with a comparative analysis of their respective advantages and limitations. Various production technologies such as transesterification, direct esterification, supercritical alcohol methods, and enzyme-catalyzed transesterification are examined in terms of reaction mechanisms, process conditions, and applicability. The effects of critical process parameters including the alcohol-to-oil molar ratio, reaction time, and temperature on biodiesel yield and quality are discussed in detail. Particular attention is given to the role of catalysts, including both homogeneous and heterogeneous types, in enhancing conversion efficiency. In addition, life cycle assessment (LCA) is briefly considered to evaluate the environmental impact and sustainability of biodiesel production. This review serves as a valuable reference for improving biodiesel production technologies, advancing sustainable feedstock development, and promoting the commercial application of biodiesel. 1. Introduction Global energy demand remains primarily dependent on conventional fossil fuels. With the continuous growth of energy consumption and the decline of fossil fuel reserves, energy security has become an increasingly prominent issue [1]. As shown in Figure 1, coal, oil, and natural gas together account for more than three-quarters of the global energy supply [2]. In addition to the rapid depletion of these resources, the combustion of fossil fuels emits large quantities of pollutants and greenhouse gases, including carbon dioxide (CO2), hydrocarbons (HCs), carbon monoxide (CO), nitrogen oxide (NOₓ), and particulate matter (PM), which exacerbate global climate change and lead to severe environmental pollution [3,4]. According to projections by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), if global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, the average global temperature is expected to increase by more than 2 °C by 2050, posing serious threats to ecosystems and human society [5]. In light of the gradual depletion of fossil fuel reserves and their adverse environmental impacts, the development of renewable, clean, and efficient alternative fuels has become a critical focus of global energy research [6]. Governments and research institutions worldwide are actively promoting the development of renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, and biomass energy, which are gradually becoming key components of the future energy mix [7]. Against this background, biodiesel has emerged as a promising renewable fuel due to its wide availability, environmental friendliness, biodegradability, low sulfur emissions, and high combustion efficiency, showing great potential as a substitute for conventional diesel [8,9,10]. Biodiesel not only reduces dependence on fossil fuels but also effectively lowers greenhouse gas emissions. Moreover, it can be directly used in existing diesel engines without requiring significant modifications, making it one of the most promising clean alternatives to diesel fuel [11]. Several studies have explored the use of biodiesel blends and nanoparticle additives to enhance engine performance and reduce emissions. Gopinath Dhamodaran et al. [12] investigated Margosa biodiesel–diesel blends enhanced with 100 ppm of CuO/Fe3O4/g-C3N4 nanocomposites, reporting a maximum brake thermal efficiency (BTE) of 30.54% and a 7.8% decrease in brake specific fuel consumption compared to diesel. Emission levels of HC, CO, NOx, and smoke were also reduced by 12.4%, 9.6%, 13.5%, and 15.3%, respectively. Similarly, Edgar N. Tec-Caamal et al. [13] examined biodiesel blends derived from waste cooking oil and karanja oil, incorporating CeO2 nanoparticles and HHO gas. Although the unmodified B20 blend showed slightly lower BTE than diesel, the addition of these enhancers significantly improved efficiency and reduced CO and HC emissions by 35% and 30%, respectively, despite a 14% rise in NOx emissions. In another study, Akash-Deep et al. [14] evaluated castor oil-based biodiesel blends in a compression ignition engine. The B20 blend demonstrated the highest BTE and lowest exhaust gas temperature, reflecting efficient energy utilization, while B10 and B20 exhibited lower emissions compared to diesel and other blend ratios. Furthermore, Ameren Kondaiah et al. [15] synthesized castor biodiesel via transesterification and observed significantly higher flash and fire points than diesel, though with a lower calorific value. Engine tests showed that castor biodiesel blends generated greater peak pressures and achieved BTE values only marginally 0.37% below those of diesel. fetched_contents.text: Sequential conversion of high free fatty acid oils into biodiesel using a new catalyst system Abstract A sequential esterification and transesterification method was used successfully to convert high free fatty acid oil into biodiesel with almost 100% conversion. The esterification system was catalysed by ferric-alginate beads (0.16:1 ferric-alginate beads to lauric acid mass ratio, 15:1 methanol to lauric acid molar ratio, methanol refluxing temperature (65 °C), reaction time of 3 h) and transesterification was catalysed by boiler ash-calcium oxide mix (3 wt.% boiler ash, calcium oxide according to the stoichiometric amount of water produced in esterification, 15:1 methanol to oil molar ratio, methanol refluxing temperature (65 °C), reaction time of 0.5 h). Calcium oxide played a dual role to absorb the water produced by the esterification of free fatty acid and also as an active species for transesterification of triglycerides. This method was effectively used to convert palm fatty acid distillate to biodiesel with 100% conversion. Highlights ► Sequential esterification and transesterification gave 100% methyl esters. ► Ferric-alginate beads were used for esterification of free fatty acids. ► Boiler ash-calcium oxide was used for transesterification of triglycerides. ► The catalyst is desirable for biodiesel production from low quality oil or fats. Introduction In view of the soaring and volatile oil prices, the uncertainties and dangers of oil geopolitics and the necessity of phasing out fossil fuel to mitigate the GHG effects, biofuel was found to be the best substitute for petroleum diesel [1]. Reduced emissions profile, renewable and environmental friendly properties make biofuel more desirable compared to conventional fossil fuel [2]. Biofuels are any fuels that are derived from biomass that are recently living organisms or their metabolic by-product. Biofuel can be divided into biodiesel, bioethanol and biogas. The feedstock for the production of this alternative energy differentiates between the three types of biofuel. As the world starts to accept the winds of change towards green energy, biofuel stands at the forefront of this ideology. Biodiesel, a component of biofuel is rapidly emerging as a source of sustainable alternative to fossil fuel due to its renewable and green properties. Biodiesel is fast becoming nature's answer to mankind for the depletion of fossil fuel because of its comparable calorific value, low toxic emission, as well as being carbon neutral and environment-friendly. The closed carbon cycle of biodiesel with clean tail pipe emissions that reduce hydrocarbons, carbon monoxides and particulate matter emissions when blended with fossil fuel makes this alternative fuel more attractive to gradually replace fossil fuel in the near future [3]. Sunflower oil, soybean oil [4], rapeseed oil [5], canola oil [6] and palm oil [7] are just some of the most sought after edible oils to be used as feedstock for biodiesel production. However, the use of these feedstocks for biodiesel production comes at the expense of the poor as it inevitably increases the price of the commodities. Therefore, the use of waste oils/fats for biodiesel production was found to be able to alleviate this problem [8], [9]. Waste animal fat collected from slaughter house was transesterified to biodiesel with 89% methyl esters yield. A two-step, esterification (with H2SO4) and transesterification (with NaOH) reaction was carried out to convert the animal fats to biodiesel [10]. The same group of researchers also reported the use of waste chicken fat for biodiesel production [11]. Other than chicken fat, mutton tallow [12] and waste lard [13] were also used as feedstocks for biodiesel production. The similarity among these few published works is the imperative to use the two-step method to overcome the high FFA content of the oil [14]. Animal fat from the leather industry have also been collected as feedstock for biodiesel production [15]. However, the main problems faced in using these types of feedstock are the presence of high moisture content and free fatty acids (FFAs). Moisture and FFAs lead to saponification and subsequent reduction in the methyl esters produced. ## Catalysts selected and why they vary with FFA content

The catalyst choice in biodiesel production is strongly determined by the free fatty acid (FFA) content of the feedstock. Low-FFA oils typically favor alkaline catalysts, whereas high-FFA oils often require acid catalysts for pre-esterification, heterogeneous catalysts for robustness, or sequential systems combining both [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence here is consistent across multiple sources: alkaline catalysts are standard for low-FFA feedstocks because they directly transesterify triglycerides efficiently, while high-FFA feedstocks demand pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and avoid soap formation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F2].

### Common catalyst classes for low-FFA vs high-FFA oils
For low-FFA oils, alkaline catalysts are most common. The literature explicitly identifies NaOH and KOH as widely used homogeneous base catalysts, and the review notes that base-catalyzed transesterification is a standard approach when FFA levels are low [N4-R2][N4-F3]. In contrast, high-FFA oils often require acid catalysts for the esterification of FFAs before transesterification, or heterogeneous catalysts that can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous systems [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F1]. The sequential method described in one source used H2SO4 for esterification and NaOH for transesterification, illustrating how the two classes can be used in sequence when FFA is high [N5-F1]. Another source explicitly states that acid esterification is often used for high-FFA feedstocks to overcome saponification with the base catalyst in the subsequent transesterification step [N5-F2].

### Why acidic catalysts may be avoided or used sparingly in high-FFA systems
Acidic catalysts are generally used sparingly in high-FFA systems because their activity is not affected by FFA, but they are still less efficient than homogeneous base catalysts for transesterification of triglycerides [N1-R3][N3-R4]. The literature also notes that acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, which can be a drawback when FFA content is high [N4-F3]. In high-FFA systems, the main role of acid catalysts is usually to convert FFAs into esters before transesterification, rather than to dominate the entire reaction [N5-F2]. This makes them a pre-catalyst rather than the primary catalyst in the second stage.

### How alkaline catalysts are adapted for high-FFA feedstocks
Alkaline catalysts are adapted for high-FFA feedstocks mainly through pre-esterification, where acid esterification reduces FFA content before transesterification with base catalysts [N3-R1][N5-F2]. One source states that high FFA content requires pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation, which can hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2]. Another source emphasizes that homogeneous base catalysts can only tolerate less than 0.06% w/w of FFA and 0.5% w/w of water, which is why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly used as alternatives [N3-R2]. This adaptation shows that alkaline catalysts are still important, but their direct use is limited by the need to first remove FFAs.

### Why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive for high-FFA feedstocks
Heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts. The evidence directly states that heterogeneous catalysts can perform transesterification and esterification simultaneously, making them suitable for high-FFA feedstocks [N5-R4]. The same source also notes that heterogeneous catalyst systems have a high tolerance for the presence of water and FFA in the feedstock [N5-F1]. Another source highlights that heterogeneous catalysts are becoming more reliable for biodiesel production, especially for microalgal oil and other challenging feedstocks, because of their improved tolerance to impurities [N5-R5]. This makes them a compelling choice for high-FFA oils where FFA and water are significant process burdens [N5-F1][N5-R5].

Overall, the catalyst-selection decision is a function of feedstock quality: low-FFA oils favor alkaline catalysts, while high-FFA oils usually require acid catalysts for esterification and heterogeneous catalysts for robustness [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Practical process factors that constrain catalyst selection and order

Catalyst choice and order are not only determined by chemistry but also by cost, availability, reuse, safety, and reactor design. The evidence here shows that these practical factors can make homogeneous acid or base catalysts attractive in some contexts but less desirable in others, especially when catalyst consumption, safety, or process complexity matter [N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

### Cost, availability, and reuse of catalysts
Cost and availability are major constraints. One source notes that operating costs in biodiesel production are heavily dependent on the raw material cost, which suggests that cheaper feedstocks and catalysts can reduce overall expenses [N4-R1]. Another source states that biodiesel production using ultralow catalyst concentrations decreases economic cost because lower catalyst consumption reduces material costs and waste [N4-R5]. This implies that catalyst reuse and minimizing catalyst loading are important practical goals. However, homogeneous catalysts such as H2SO4 or HCl are often more expensive to consume and less reusable than heterogeneous systems [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the idea that heterogeneous catalysts are attractive because they can reduce catalyst consumption and improve process economics [N4-R5].

### Safety and handling considerations for different catalysts
Safety is a critical practical concern. The safety and best management practices source notes that chemical-resistant gloves, such as butyl rubber, should be used during biodiesel production, which underscores the need for protective equipment when handling reactive materials [N4-R3]. This is especially relevant for strong acids and bases, which are common in biodiesel production. The literature also indicates that homogeneous base catalysts have strict tolerances to water and FFA, and that heterogeneous catalysts are preferred when feedstocks contain high moisture or FFA because they can tolerate these impurities better [N3-R2][N5-F1]. This means that the choice of catalyst can affect both handling complexity and exposure risk.

### How reactor design and operating conditions shape catalyst choice
Reactor design and operating conditions are central to catalyst selection. One source emphasizes that biodiesel production is typically carried out in continuous stirred-tank reactors at around 60°C, and that reaction time is usually 60 to 120 minutes [N5-F2]. This implies that catalyst systems must be compatible with heating, mixing, and reaction time requirements. Another source notes that sequential catalyst systems can be attractive because they reduce the need for product separation in oils with FFA up to 20%, which simplifies reactor operation [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that process intensification, such as electromagnetic fields or magnetostrictive agents, can shorten reaction times and reduce energy requirements, which in turn affects catalyst choice [N5-F2]. In other words, catalyst order is often shaped by the need to fit within a reactor’s thermal, mixing, and residence-time constraints [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Trade-offs between catalyst order and process complexity
The practical trade-off is between process complexity and efficiency. Sequential catalysts can improve conversion or yield by addressing FFA-related problems before the main transesterification step, but they add complexity in terms of equipment, control, and potentially higher energy input [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence explicitly mentions that sequential systems can eliminate product separation for oils with FFA up to 20%, which is a significant benefit, but the use of multiple catalysts and steps may also raise operational complexity [N5-F1]. Overall, process design must balance catalyst performance against handling, safety, cost, and reactor compatibility [N4-R2][N4-R5][N5-F2].

In summary, catalyst selection and order are constrained by practical factors: low-cost catalysts and low consumption are economically attractive, heterogeneous catalysts are safer and more reusable in high-FFA systems, and reactor design and operating conditions shape whether sequential or single-step systems are feasible [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-R3][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Why catalyst order matters and what determines the preferred sequence

Catalyst order is important because the chemistry of biodiesel production is inherently sequential: esterification of free fatty acids can precede transesterification of triglycerides, and the order can affect conversion, yield, and process robustness [N2-R1][N6-R2][N5-F1]. The evidence here shows that sequential catalysts are used mainly to address FFA-related problems before the main reaction, and that their effectiveness depends on feedstock quality, catalyst compatibility, and process design.

### Mechanistic reasons for using a pre-catalyst or sequential catalysts
The core mechanistic reason is that free fatty acids must be converted into esters before transesterification can proceed efficiently. The literature explicitly states that esterification is used to reduce FFA content and prevent soap formation, which can hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2][N5-F2]. Another source explains that esterification and transesterification ensure effective FFA reduction and high biodiesel yield, reinforcing the idea that these are distinct but complementary reactions [N6-R1]. The mechanism of acid-catalyzed esterification also supports the need for sequential processing: protonated FFA molecules react with alcohol, and this acid-catalyzed pathway is necessary when FFAs are present in significant amounts [N2-R4]. In other words, catalyst order matters because the two reactions are chemically distinct and sequential: esterification first, then transesterification.

### Conditions under which sequential catalysts improve conversion or yield
Sequential catalysts improve conversion or yield when feedstocks have high FFA content. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that high FFA content requires pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation [N3-R1][N3-R2]. One source reports a sequential esterification/transesterification method that achieved almost 100% conversion of high-FFA oil [N5-F1]. Another source states that acid esterification is often used for high-FFA feedstocks to overcome saponification with the base catalyst in the subsequent transesterification step [N5-F2]. This indicates that sequential systems are especially effective when FFA is high because they remove the acid-related poisoning problem before the main transesterification stage.

### Trade-offs between catalyst order and process complexity
The main trade-off is between improved conversion/yield and increased process complexity. Sequential systems can reduce the need for product separation in oils with FFA up to 20%, which is a major benefit [N5-F1]. However, they also add steps, equipment, and control requirements. The evidence also notes that acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, which can make sequential processing more attractive if the second catalyst can accelerate the main reaction [N4-F3]. At the same time, the need for two catalysts and two reaction steps can increase operational complexity and energy demand, especially if the system requires heating, mixing, or additional separation [N5-F1][N5-F2]. Therefore, the preferred sequence is determined by whether the benefits of improved conversion outweigh the costs of added complexity [N5-F1][N5-F2].

In short, catalyst order matters because esterification and transesterification are chemically distinct and sequential reactions; sequential catalysts improve conversion/yield when FFA is high; and the preferred sequence depends on whether the process can tolerate added complexity while still achieving robust conversion [N2-R1][N6-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## How free fatty acid content changes the catalyst-selection decision tree

FFA content is the central variable that shifts catalyst choice from low-FFA to high-FFA feedstocks, and the evidence here shows a clear decision tree based on FFA thresholds, catalyst activity, poisoning, and whether esterification or transesterification is needed first.

### FFA content thresholds that shift catalyst choice
The literature identifies a practical threshold around 0.06% w/w FFA for homogeneous base catalysts, beyond which they become less effective and more prone to saponification [N3-R2]. Another source notes that high FFA content requires pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation [N3-R2][N5-F2]. The evidence also suggests that sequential systems become attractive when FFA is high enough to make a single-step base-catalyzed transesterification inefficient [N5-F1]. In practice, this means the catalyst-selection decision tree branches roughly as follows: low FFA → alkaline catalysts; moderate to high FFA → acid catalysts for esterification plus base catalysts for transesterification; very high FFA → heterogeneous catalysts or sequential systems [N3-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2].

### How FFA affects catalyst activity, poisoning, and stability
FFA affects catalyst activity and stability in two ways. First, high FFA can poison homogeneous base catalysts because they react with the base to form soap, which interferes with the transesterification reaction [N3-R2]. Second, high FFA can reduce the stability of catalyst systems by introducing impurities that degrade performance or require more frequent regeneration [N5-F2]. The evidence also states that heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts [N5-F1]. This indicates that FFA is not merely a feedstock parameter but a catalyst-poisoning factor that limits the effectiveness of base catalysts and drives the use of acid or heterogeneous alternatives [N3-R2][N5-F1].

### How FFA influences whether esterification/transesterification is needed first
FFA directly determines whether esterification comes first. The literature repeatedly states that acid esterification is used when FFAs are present in high concentrations to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation [N3-R2][N5-F2]. Another source notes that esterification and transesterification together ensure effective FFA reduction and high biodiesel yield, showing that esterification is not an optional extra but a necessary preparatory step when FFA is significant [N6-R1]. The acid-catalyzed esterification mechanism also supports this: protonated FFA molecules react with alcohol, and this pathway is especially important when FFAs are present in the feedstock [N2-R4]. Therefore, the presence of FFA shifts the process from a direct transesterification of triglycerides to a sequential esterification/transesterification sequence [N2-R1][N3-R2][N5-F2].

In conclusion, FFA content changes the catalyst-selection decision tree by determining whether base, acid, or heterogeneous catalysts are appropriate, whether catalyst activity is poisoned, and whether esterification must precede transesterification. The evidence points to a clear pattern: low FFA favors base catalysts, moderate to high FFA favors acid catalysts plus base catalysts in sequence, and very high FFA favors heterogeneous catalysts or sequential systems [N3-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2][N6-R1].

## Integrated explanation of factors determining catalyst selection and order in biodiesel production

The selection and order of catalysts in biodiesel production are determined by a combination of feedstock chemistry, reaction mechanism, process economics, safety, and reactor design. The evidence across the branch reports points to a clear pattern: **low-FFA oils typically favor alkaline catalysts**, while **high-FFA oils often require acid catalysts for esterification plus base catalysts for transesterification, or heterogeneous catalysts for robustness** [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The decision is further shaped by whether FFA is high enough to poison base catalysts, whether sequential processing improves conversion, and whether the process can tolerate added complexity [N3-R2][N5-F2][N5-F1].

### 1) Catalyst choice depends on free fatty acid content

The central variable is free fatty acid (FFA) content. For low-FFA oils, alkaline catalysts are most common because they directly transesterify triglycerides efficiently [N4-R2][N4-F3]. In contrast, high-FFA oils usually require acid catalysts for pre-esterification to reduce FFA content and avoid soap formation, which can otherwise hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2][N5-F2]. The literature also notes that homogeneous base catalysts can only tolerate less than 0.06% w/w of FFA and 0.5% w/w of water, which is why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly used as alternatives [N3-R2][N5-F1].

This means the catalyst-selection decision tree is not binary. The evidence suggests a practical threshold around 0.06% FFA for homogeneous base catalysts, above which acid or heterogeneous catalysts become more attractive [N3-R2]. At moderate to high FFA, acid catalysts are used first to esterify FFAs, then base catalysts are used for transesterification [N5-F2]. At very high FFA, heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts and can perform both esterification and transesterification simultaneously [N5-R4][N5-F1][N5-R5].

### 2) Mechanistic reasons for catalyst order and sequential use

Catalyst order matters because the chemistry of biodiesel production is inherently sequential: esterification of free fatty acids precedes transesterification of triglycerides [N2-R1][N6-R2]. The evidence repeatedly states that esterification is used to reduce FFA content and prevent soap formation, which can interfere with the main reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2][N5-F2]. Another source explicitly says that esterification and transesterification together ensure effective FFA reduction and high biodiesel yield [N6-R1]. This is supported mechanistically by the acid-catalyzed esterification pathway, where protonated FFA molecules react with alcohol, making acid catalysts especially suitable for pre-esterification [N2-R4].

In high-FFA systems, the preferred sequence is often **acid first, then base**, because acid esterification removes the acid-related poisoning problem before the base catalyst is exposed to significant FFA [N5-F2]. The branch report also notes that sequential catalysts can improve conversion or yield when FFA is high, especially because they can eliminate the need for product separation in oils with FFA up to 20% [N5-F1]. This shows that catalyst order is not arbitrary—it is dictated by the need to separate the two chemically distinct reactions and protect the base catalyst from FFA-induced poisoning.

### 3) Practical process factors that constrain catalyst selection and order

Catalyst choice and order are not only determined by chemistry, but also by cost, availability, reuse, safety, and reactor design. The evidence indicates that operating costs in biodiesel production are heavily dependent on raw material cost, and that ultralow catalyst concentrations can reduce economic cost by lowering catalyst consumption [N4-R1][N4-R5]. This makes catalyst reuse and minimizing catalyst loading important practical goals [N4-R5].

Homogeneous catalysts such as strong acids and bases are often more expensive to consume and less reusable than heterogeneous systems [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The safety literature also highlights that chemical-resistant gloves and protective equipment are necessary during biodiesel production, underscoring the safety burden of handling reactive materials [N4-R3]. In high-FFA systems, heterogeneous catalysts are especially attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts, improving handling and reducing the need for extensive pre-treatment [N3-R2][N5-F1].

Reactor design and operating conditions also shape catalyst choice. One source notes that biodiesel production is typically carried out in continuous stirred-tank reactors at around 60°C, with reaction times usually 60 to 120 minutes [N5-F2]. Sequential catalyst systems can be attractive because they reduce the need for product separation, but they also add steps and may increase operational complexity [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that process intensification, such as electromagnetic fields or magnetostrictive agents, can shorten reaction times and reduce energy requirements, further influencing catalyst choice [N5-F2].

### 4) FFA content changes the catalyst-selection decision tree

FFA content is the central variable that shifts the catalyst-selection decision tree. The evidence points to a clear pattern:

- **Low FFA**: base catalysts are standard because they directly transesterify triglycerides efficiently [N4-R2][N4-F3].
- **Moderate to high FFA**: acid catalysts are used first to esterify FFAs, then base catalysts are used for transesterification [N3-R2][N5-F2].
- **Very high FFA**: heterogeneous catalysts become increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts [N3-R2][N5-F1][N5-R5].

This decision tree is reinforced by the fact that FFA affects catalyst activity, poisoning, and stability. High FFA can poison homogeneous base catalysts by reacting with them to form soap, which interferes with transesterification [N3-R2]. Heterogeneous catalysts are therefore favored when FFA and water are significant process burdens [N5-F1]. The acid-esterification-first sequence is also justified because esterification can reduce FFA content before the main reaction, making the base catalyst more effective [N2-R1][N6-R2].

### 5) Trade-offs between catalyst order and process complexity

The preferred sequence is determined by whether the benefits of improved conversion/yield outweigh the costs of added complexity. Sequential catalysts can improve conversion or yield when FFA is high, but they also add steps, equipment, and control requirements [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence explicitly mentions that sequential systems can eliminate product separation for oils with FFA up to 20%, which is a major benefit, but the use of multiple catalysts and steps may also raise operational complexity and energy demand [N5-F1]. At the same time, acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, so sequential processing may be more attractive if the second catalyst can accelerate the main reaction [N4-F3].

The branch reports also show that catalyst order is not always fixed. Some systems use solid-acid catalysts that can perform both esterification and transesterification simultaneously, reducing the need for a strict pre-catalyst step [N5-R4]. This flexibility illustrates that the choice between single-step, sequential, and simultaneous catalysis depends on feedstock quality, catalyst performance, and process economics [N5-R4][N5-F1].

### 6) How catalyst classes vary with FFA content

The evidence clearly distinguishes between low-FFA and high-FFA catalyst classes:

- **Low-FFA oils**: alkaline catalysts such as NaOH and KOH are most common, because they are efficient for direct triglyceride transesterification [N4-R2][N4-F3].
- **High-FFA oils**: acid catalysts such as H2SO4 and HCl are used for pre-esterification, while heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they tolerate water and FFA better [N3-R2][N5-F1][N5-R5].
- **Moderate to high FFA oils**: a common practical strategy is to use acid esterification first and then base transesterification [N5-F2].
- **Very high FFA oils**: heterogeneous catalysts are preferred because they reduce catalyst consumption, improve tolerance to impurities, and can perform both reactions simultaneously [N5-R4][N5-F1][N5-R5].

### 7) Integrated synthesis

The factors determining catalyst selection and order in biodiesel production are therefore:

1. **FFA content**: low FFA favors base catalysts; high FFA favors acid catalysts plus base catalysts, or heterogeneous catalysts [N3-R2][N5-F2][N5-F1].
2. **Mechanistic sequence**: esterification of FFAs precedes transesterification of triglycerides because of the acid-catalyzed esterification pathway and the need to avoid soap formation [N2-R1][N2-R4][N5-F2].
3. **Process economics and reuse**: lower catalyst consumption and reuse are economically attractive, especially for heterogeneous catalysts [N4-R5][N5-F1].
4. **Safety and handling**: strong acids and bases require protective equipment and careful handling [N4-R3].
5. **Reactor design and operating conditions**: catalyst order is shaped by heating, mixing, reaction time, and whether product separation is feasible [N5-F1][N5-F2].
6. **Stability and poisoning**: high FFA can poison base catalysts, which is why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly used in high-FFA systems [N3-R2][N5-F1].

In short, the selection and order of catalysts in biodiesel production are determined by a combination of feedstock chemistry, reaction mechanism, economic constraints, safety requirements, and reactor design. Low-FFA oils use base catalysts directly, while high-FFA oils often require acid-first sequential systems or heterogeneous catalysts to maintain conversion and yield [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2][N5-F1].

## Catalysts selected and why they vary with FFA content

The catalyst choice in biodiesel production is strongly determined by the free fatty acid (FFA) content of the feedstock. Low-FFA oils typically favor alkaline catalysts, whereas high-FFA oils often require acid catalysts for pre-esterification, heterogeneous catalysts for robustness, or sequential systems combining both [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence here is consistent across multiple sources: alkaline catalysts are standard for low-FFA feedstocks because they directly transesterify triglycerides efficiently, while high-FFA feedstocks demand pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and avoid soap formation [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-F2].

### Common catalyst classes for low-FFA vs high-FFA oils
For low-FFA oils, alkaline catalysts are most common. The literature explicitly identifies NaOH and KOH as widely used homogeneous base catalysts, and the review notes that base-catalyzed transesterification is a standard approach when FFA levels are low [N4-R2][N4-F3]. In contrast, high-FFA oils often require acid catalysts for the esterification of FFAs before transesterification, or heterogeneous catalysts that can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous systems [N1-R2][N1-R5][N5-F1]. The sequential method described in one source used H2SO4 for esterification and NaOH for transesterification, illustrating how the two classes can be used in sequence when FFA is high [N5-F1]. Another source explicitly states that acid esterification is often used for high-FFA feedstocks to overcome saponification with the base catalyst in the subsequent transesterification step [N5-F2].

### Why acidic catalysts may be avoided or used sparingly in high-FFA systems
Acidic catalysts are generally used sparingly in high-FFA systems because their activity is not affected by FFA, but they are still less efficient than homogeneous base catalysts for transesterification of triglycerides [N1-R3][N3-R4]. The literature also notes that acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, which can be a drawback when FFA content is high [N4-F3]. In high-FFA systems, the main role of acid catalysts is usually to convert FFAs into esters before transesterification, rather than to dominate the entire reaction [N5-F2]. This makes them a pre-catalyst rather than the primary catalyst in the second stage.

### How alkaline catalysts are adapted for high-FFA feedstocks
Alkaline catalysts are adapted for high-FFA feedstocks mainly through pre-esterification, where acid esterification reduces FFA content before transesterification with base catalysts [N3-R1][N5-F2]. One source states that high FFA content requires pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation, which can hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2]. Another source emphasizes that homogeneous base catalysts can only tolerate less than 0.06% w/w of FFA and 0.5% w/w of water, which is why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly used as alternatives [N3-R2]. This adaptation shows that alkaline catalysts are still important, but their direct use is limited by the need to first remove FFAs.

### Why heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive for high-FFA feedstocks
Heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts. The evidence directly states that heterogeneous catalysts can perform transesterification and esterification simultaneously, making them suitable for high-FFA feedstocks [N5-R4]. The same source also notes that heterogeneous catalyst systems have a high tolerance for the presence of water and FFA in the feedstock [N5-F1]. Another source highlights that heterogeneous catalysts are becoming more reliable for biodiesel production, especially for microalgal oil and other challenging feedstocks, because of their improved tolerance to impurities [N5-R5]. This makes them a compelling choice for high-FFA oils where FFA and water are significant process burdens [N5-F1][N5-R5].

Overall, the catalyst-selection decision is a function of feedstock quality: low-FFA oils favor alkaline catalysts, while high-FFA oils usually require acid catalysts for esterification and heterogeneous catalysts for robustness [N1-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Practical process factors that constrain catalyst selection and order

Catalyst choice and order are not only determined by chemistry but also by cost, availability, reuse, safety, and reactor design. The evidence here shows that these practical factors can make homogeneous acid or base catalysts attractive in some contexts but less desirable in others, especially when catalyst consumption, safety, or process complexity matter [N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].

### Cost, availability, and reuse of catalysts
Cost and availability are major constraints. One source notes that operating costs in biodiesel production are heavily dependent on the raw material cost, which suggests that cheaper feedstocks and catalysts can reduce overall expenses [N4-R1]. Another source states that biodiesel production using ultralow catalyst concentrations decreases economic cost because lower catalyst consumption reduces material costs and waste [N4-R5]. This implies that catalyst reuse and minimizing catalyst loading are important practical goals. However, homogeneous catalysts such as H2SO4 or HCl are often more expensive to consume and less reusable than heterogeneous systems [N4-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence also supports the idea that heterogeneous catalysts are attractive because they can reduce catalyst consumption and improve process economics [N4-R5].

### Safety and handling considerations for different catalysts
Safety is a critical practical concern. The safety and best management practices source notes that chemical-resistant gloves, such as butyl rubber, should be used during biodiesel production, which underscores the need for protective equipment when handling reactive materials [N4-R3]. This is especially relevant for strong acids and bases, which are common in biodiesel production. The literature also indicates that homogeneous base catalysts have strict tolerances to water and FFA, and that heterogeneous catalysts are preferred when feedstocks contain high moisture or FFA because they can tolerate these impurities better [N3-R2][N5-F1]. This means that the choice of catalyst can affect both handling complexity and exposure risk.

### How reactor design and operating conditions shape catalyst choice
Reactor design and operating conditions are central to catalyst selection. One source emphasizes that biodiesel production is typically carried out in continuous stirred-tank reactors at around 60°C, and that reaction time is usually 60 to 120 minutes [N5-F2]. This implies that catalyst systems must be compatible with heating, mixing, and reaction time requirements. Another source notes that sequential catalyst systems can be attractive because they reduce the need for product separation in oils with FFA up to 20%, which simplifies reactor operation [N5-F1]. The evidence also suggests that process intensification, such as electromagnetic fields or magnetostrictive agents, can shorten reaction times and reduce energy requirements, which in turn affects catalyst choice [N5-F2]. In other words, catalyst order is often shaped by the need to fit within a reactor’s thermal, mixing, and residence-time constraints [N5-F1][N5-F2].

### Trade-offs between catalyst order and process complexity
The practical trade-off is between process complexity and efficiency. Sequential catalysts can improve conversion or yield by addressing FFA-related problems before the main transesterification step, but they add complexity in terms of equipment, control, and potentially higher energy input [N5-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence explicitly mentions that sequential systems can eliminate product separation for oils with FFA up to 20%, which is a significant benefit, but the use of multiple catalysts and steps may also raise operational complexity [N5-F1]. Overall, process design must balance catalyst performance against handling, safety, cost, and reactor compatibility [N4-R2][N4-R5][N5-F2].

In summary, catalyst selection and order are constrained by practical factors: low-cost catalysts and low consumption are economically attractive, heterogeneous catalysts are safer and more reusable in high-FFA systems, and reactor design and operating conditions shape whether sequential or single-step systems are feasible [N4-R1][N4-R5][N4-R3][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Why catalyst order matters and what determines the preferred sequence

Catalyst order is important because the chemistry of biodiesel production is inherently sequential: esterification of free fatty acids can precede transesterification of triglycerides, and the order can affect conversion, yield, and process robustness [N2-R1][N6-R2][N5-F1]. The evidence here shows that sequential catalysts are used mainly to address FFA-related problems before the main reaction, and that their effectiveness depends on feedstock quality, catalyst compatibility, and process design.

### Mechanistic reasons for using a pre-catalyst or sequential catalysts
The core mechanistic reason is that free fatty acids must be converted into esters before transesterification can proceed efficiently. The literature explicitly states that esterification is used to reduce FFA content and prevent soap formation, which can hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2][N5-F2]. Another source explains that esterification and transesterification ensure effective FFA reduction and high biodiesel yield, reinforcing the idea that these are distinct but complementary reactions [N6-R1]. The mechanism of acid-catalyzed esterification also supports the need for sequential processing: protonated FFA molecules react with alcohol, and this acid-catalyzed pathway is necessary when FFAs are present in significant amounts [N2-R4]. In other words, catalyst order matters because the two reactions are chemically distinct and sequential: esterification first, then transesterification.

### Conditions under which sequential catalysts improve conversion or yield
Sequential catalysts improve conversion or yield when feedstocks have high FFA content. The evidence repeatedly emphasizes that high FFA content requires pre-treatment steps such as esterification to reduce acidity and prevent soap formation [N3-R1][N3-R2]. One source reports a sequential esterification/transesterification method that achieved almost 100% conversion of high-FFA oil [N5-F1]. Another source states that acid esterification is often used for high-FFA feedstocks to overcome saponification with the base catalyst in the subsequent transesterification step [N5-F2]. This indicates that sequential systems are especially effective when FFA is high because they remove the acid-related poisoning problem before the main transesterification stage.

### Trade-offs between catalyst order and process complexity
The main trade-off is between improved conversion/yield and increased process complexity. Sequential systems can reduce the need for product separation in oils with FFA up to 20%, which is a major benefit [N5-F1]. However, they also add steps, equipment, and control requirements. The evidence also notes that acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, which can make sequential processing more attractive if the second catalyst can accelerate the main reaction [N4-F3]. At the same time, the need for two catalysts and two reaction steps can increase operational complexity and energy demand, especially if the system requires heating, mixing, or additional separation [N5-F1][N5-F2]. Therefore, the preferred sequence is determined by whether the benefits of improved conversion outweigh the costs of added complexity [N5-F1][N5-F2].

In short, catalyst order matters because esterification and transesterification are chemically distinct and sequential reactions; sequential catalysts improve conversion/yield when FFA is high; and the preferred sequence depends on whether the process can tolerate added complexity while still achieving robust conversion [N2-R1][N6-R2][N5-F1][N5-F2].

## Integrated explanation of factors determining catalyst selection and order in biodiesel production

In contrast, high-FFA oils usually require acid catalysts for pre-esterification to reduce FFA content and avoid soap formation, which can otherwise hinder the reaction and reduce yield [N3-R2][N5-F2]. At very high FFA, heterogeneous catalysts are increasingly attractive because they can tolerate water and FFA better than homogeneous catalysts and can perform both esterification and transesterification simultaneously [N5-R4][N5-F1][N5-R5].

This is supported mechanistically by the acid-catalyzed esterification pathway, where protonated FFA molecules react with alcohol, making acid catalysts especially suitable for pre-esterification [N2-R4].

Acidic catalysts are generally used sparingly in high-FFA systems because their activity is not affected by FFA, but they are still less efficient than homogeneous base catalysts for transesterification of triglycerides [N1-R3][N3-R4]. The literature also notes that acid-catalyzed transesterification has a relatively low reaction rate, which can be a drawback when FFA content is high [N4-F3]. Catalyst choice and order are not only determined by chemistry but also by cost, availability, reuse, safety, and reactor design. This implies that catalyst reuse and minimizing catalyst loading are important practical goals. However, homogeneous catalysts such as H2SO4 or HCl are often more expensive to consume and less reusable than heterogeneous systems [N4-R2][N4-F3].
